cultivar: Various, including Tieguanyin, Huangdan, Benshan, Maoxie, Meizhan, Foshou, Baiya Qilan
processing: Mostly ball-rolled and, in the common fragrant style, lightly oxidised with little roast; traditional styles take more oxidation and roasting.
harvest_season: Spring and autumn are the prized pickings in Anxi.
appearance_dry: Tight rolled pellets, from jade green in the light style to dark brown in the roasted style.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green in the fragrant style, gold to amber when roasted.
appearance_wet: Whole leaves open from the pellet, greener with slight red edges in the light style.
taste_profile: In the fragrant style, orchid-like florals with a fresh, quickly returning sweetness; roasted lots turn warmer and fruitier.

brewing.notes: A family of teas. Rinse quickly to open the pellets, then use hot water with short steeps, and go a little shorter on green styles.

vintage_note: This is a regional family and not one product. Its teas are normally sold by plant, season and year, with the light style best drunk within about a year. Roasted and aged lots are separate goods and should say so.
description:
Minnan oolong means oolong from southern Fujian, with Anxi at the centre and Tie Guan Yin as its best-known tea. Yongchun Foshou and Pinghe Baiya Qilan belong too, as do Anxi's many other plants.

The group usually means rolled pellets. The dominant modern style is oxidised lightly and hardly roasted, so it comes out green and floral, while traditional styles go further and carry roast.

That makes this a family with two moods. Fragrant lots are orchid-like and fresh with a sweet aftertaste; roasted lots are warmer and rounder. Use hot water for both, and shorten steeps for the pale ones.

Buy by plant and place, since Minnan is only a regional label. Remember that Anxi plants other than Tie Guan Yin are honest teas on their own, and only a problem when sold under the wrong name.
history:
The north and south split is a long-standing way of classing Fujian oolong. Anxi's own trade classing dates from the 1950s, when inspection bodies divided its oolong into Tie Guan Yin, se zhong and oolong.

Little is documented about when the term Minnan oolong first came into use. In recent decades the light style has been the common face of the group, though traditional making has regained ground.
